planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; this compact collector's species scorches quickly under direct hot sun.

directions: Native to rocky slopes near Ladismith in South Africa's Western Cape, this small stemless rosette carries dark olive to purplish-brown leaves whose translucent tips are etched with fine, pale longitudinal lines that intensify in strong light. Pot in a gritty, mineral-heavy mix and keep in bright indirect light, since intense direct sun can turn the foliage an unattractively tight reddish-bronze while deep shade dulls its coloring and window patterning. It offsets slowly to form small clumps over several years, so division for propagation should wait until offsets have developed their own root systems. Water only once the mix has dried out fully, and reduce watering further in winter when growth slows.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; a classic collector's window haworthia from South Africa's Little Karoo.

directions: This low, stemless rosette produces broad, incurved, triangular leaves whose blunt tips form flattened, semi-translucent windows crossed with fine reticulate veining, a feature that lets light reach the photosynthetic tissue below the soil line in its native rocky Little Karoo habitat. Keep it in bright indirect light in a lean, fast-draining succulent mix, since the compact rosette can flatten and lose its tight symmetry in low light while harsh direct sun dulls the window clarity. It stays mostly solitary or offsets only sparingly, so most propagation is done by carefully removing and rooting any basal offsets rather than frequent division. Let the mix dry completely between waterings and cut back further once winter dormancy sets in.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; a highly variable Cape species prized for its many distinct forms.

directions: Found around Bredasdorp and Napier in the Western Cape, this small stemless species forms neat rosettes of pointed, often purplish-green leaves edged with fine translucent teeth and semi-translucent tips that vary considerably in pattern and color from one population to the next, which is part of its appeal to collectors. Grow in bright indirect light in a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, since the leaf coloring intensifies attractively in strong light without direct midday sun scorching the foliage. It clumps slowly by offsets, eventually forming a tight cluster of rosettes that can be divided once new offsets have rooted on their own. Water only after the potting mix has dried completely, tapering off further during the cooler winter rest period.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; prized for the fine longitudinal lines etched into its leaf windows.

directions: Native to the Riversdale district of the Western Cape, this compact rosette carries firm, dark green to purplish leaves whose translucent tips are marked with distinct pale longitudinal striping, giving each leaf a subtly striped, almost etched look. Keep it in bright indirect light and a lean, mineral-rich succulent mix, since it naturally grows tucked among rocks and low scrub where the intense midday sun is filtered, and direct exposure indoors can bleach or scorch the leaf tips. It offsets gradually into a tight, low cluster rather than spreading widely, so propagation is best done by removing well-rooted offsets rather than aggressive division. Water thoroughly but infrequently, letting the mix dry out completely between waterings, especially through winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or warm-climate container succulent in bright light; tolerates more direct sun than most soft-leaved haworthias once acclimated.

directions: Widespread across South Africa's Western and Eastern Cape, this species builds narrow, upright columns from tightly packed, triangular leaves arranged in three ranks that spiral tightly around the stem, giving it a distinctive stacked, pagoda-like silhouette unlike the flat rosettes of most related haworthias. Its rough, tuberculate leaf surface and hard texture let it handle brighter light than soft window-leaved Haworthia species, so a spot with several hours of gentle morning or filtered sun suits it well in a coarse, fast-draining cactus mix. Older columns lean or branch from the base over time and produce basal offsets that can be separated and rooted once they have their own roots. Allow the mix to dry completely between waterings, since the thick leaves store enough moisture to tolerate extended dry spells.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or container succulent in bright light with some direct sun tolerated; its grey-green leaves hold color best with strong light.

directions: This Eastern Cape species forms an upright, fan-shaped arrangement of firm, sword-shaped leaves with a distinctive grey-green, glaucous bloom that gives the plant its species name and sets it apart from the glossier greens of related zebra haworthias. It tolerates brighter light than many of its soft-leaved relatives, so a spot with bright indirect light and a little direct morning sun keeps the leaf color at its bluest without the bronzing that comes from overly intense exposure. Plant divisions in a coarse, fast-draining succulent mix, and expect the clump to slowly send up new fans from the base, forming a loose colony over a few growing seasons. Water deeply but only once the mix has dried out completely, tapering off through the cooler winter months.

planting.note: Grow as a shaded houseplant or understory container succulent in bright indirect light; one of the largest gasteria species, eventually needing a sizeable pot.

directions: Native to coastal forest and bushveld margins of KwaZulu-Natal, this is among the largest gasteria species, starting as young plants with flat, two-ranked, tongue-shaped leaves before maturing into a bold, spiraling rosette of thick, dark green leaves mottled with pale spots. Because it grows naturally in the dappled shade of forest understories, it prefers bright indirect light rather than direct sun and thrives with the deeper shade tolerance typical of forest-dwelling gasterias. Pot in a fast-draining succulent mix with a somewhat larger container than most gasterias require, since mature rosettes can become substantial, and repot as the plant outgrows its base. Water thoroughly then let the mix dry out before watering again, and separate rooted basal offsets to propagate new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light or light shade in a fast-draining succulent mix; stays compact and clusters readily for a full dish-garden look.

directions: This compact Eastern Cape species from the Humansdorp-to-Grahamstown region forms neat, two-ranked fans of thick, dark green leaves densely covered in small silvery-white spots, living up to its species name of pulchra, meaning beautiful. It naturally grows tucked beneath rocks and shrubs, so bright indirect light or dappled shade suits it better than direct sun, which can wash out the crisp spotting and give the leaves an overly bronzed look. Pot offsets in a lean, fast-draining succulent mix, and expect the plant to cluster readily into a dense colony of small fans, making it a good candidate for a shallow succulent bowl. Water only once the mix is fully dry, and reduce watering further during the winter rest period.
